title_en: Beijing iQIYI Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen JuWangShi Technology Co., Ltd. — other unfair competition dispute

full_text_en:
Beijing iQiyi Technology Co., Ltd. v. Shenzhen Juwangshi Technology Co., Ltd. — dispute over other unfair competition

Ruling Summary

The act of a person developing and operating relevant software to achieve the function of directly watching videos from other online video platforms without having to watch pre-roll advertisements violates the principle of good faith and damages the legitimate rights and interests of other online video platforms in obtaining commercial benefits based on their legitimate business models, thus constituting unfair competition.

Plaintiff: Beijing iQiyi Technology Co., Ltd., domiciled at Haidian North First Street, Haidian District, Beijing.
Legal Representative: Geng Xiaohua, Executive Director of the company.

Defendant: Shenzhen Juwangshi Technology Co., Ltd., domiciled at Bantian Street, Longgang District, Shenzhen, Guangdong Province.
Legal Representative: Hu Wenshen, Executive Director of the company.

The plaintiff, Beijing iQiyi Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as iQiyi), filed a lawsuit with the Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai against the defendant, Shenzhen Juwangshi Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Juwangshi), over a dispute concerning other unfair competition.

The plaintiff iQiyi alleged that it is the legitimate operator of "iQiyi," a well-known large online video platform in China. Through this platform, it provides video-on-demand services to end-users on the network, and also provides advertisement production and publishing services to industry advertisers. Users obtain free video content at the cost of watching video advertisements, and iQiyi derives its main operating revenue from advertising fees charged to advertisers, thereby achieving profitability. The defendant Juwangshi developed the "VST All-in-One" software and provided the software for download and operation through its official website and other channels. This software has a "video ad filtering function." After installing the software, users could directly watch video content from the iQiyi platform through the software without watching video advertisements. This led to a decrease in traffic to the iQiyi website and downloads of its media player, reduced the exposure rate of advertisements placed by advertisers on the iQiyi platform, thereby harming iQiyi's interests and infringing upon its legitimate rights. Therefore, iQiyi requested the court to order: 1. Juwangshi to compensate iQiyi for economic losses of RMB 992,000 (all currency below is in RMB), attorney's fees of RMB 50,000, and notarization fees of RMB 14,250; 2. Juwangshi to publish a statement on the top of the homepage of its official website (http://www.91vst.com/) for 72 consecutive hours to eliminate the impact of its unfair competition act.

The defendant Juwangshi argued that: It is not in the same industry as iQiyi and there is no competitive relationship between them. The fact that playing videos sourced from iQiyi through the "VST All-in-One" software does not play the pre-roll advertisements is because the video content and the advertisement content are from two different sources. Juwangshi can only obtain the video content and cannot capture the pre-roll advertisements. It did not use technical means to block iQiyi's pre-roll advertisements; the technology it used is innovative and neutral and does not constitute unfair competition. Accordingly, Juwangshi requested the court to dismiss all of iQiyi's claims.

The Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai found the following facts in the trial of first instance:

The plaintiff iQiyi was established on March 27, 2007. It is a well-known domestic video content provider, providing video playback services to network users through the "iQiyi" website (www.iqiyi.com), computer clients, and mobile platform clients such as Android and Apple. iQiyi mainly relies on the "advertising + free video" business model (i.e., playing advertisements before video content to collect advertising fees, with users obtaining free video watching by watching pre-roll advertisements of varying lengths) or a membership fee model (where users pay a fee to become members and can watch videos without watching pre-roll advertisements). It uses advertising fees and membership fees to pay for video copyrights, bandwidth, promotion, and other expenses to maintain its normal operations.

The defendant Juwangshi was established on November 22, 2013. The "VST All-in-One" software it developed and operates aggregates content from eighteen video websites, including the plaintiff's iQiyi website. It is a client software installable on Android platforms such as PADs, mobile phones, TV set-top boxes, and smart TVs.

From May 4, 2014 to March 26, 2015, the plaintiff iQiyi, through multiple notarizations, demonstrated that after installing Juwangshi's VST All-in-One software, video content from the iQiyi website could be directly played via media such as smart TVs, Tmall Magic Boxes connected to televisions, and smart phones, without playing the pre-roll advertisements.

On April 8, 2015, the plaintiff iQiyi, through notarization, used the "Wireshark" software to demonstrate the video playback principle. After a user sends a request to watch video content to iQiyi's server, the server determines the platform source of the request based on the client code (i.e., the SRC value) in the request, retrieves a corresponding key (i.e., the Key value) for the video data interface, combines it with the access time (i.e., the TimeID) and the video ID (i.e., the VideoID) from the access request, generates an SC value using the MD5 encryption algorithm in the order TimeID+Key+VideoID. If this SC value matches the SC value generated in the access request, verification passes, and the server pushes the requested content to the user. The video source data captured by the "Wireshark" software only showed the access time (TimeID), video ID (VideoID), client code (SRC value), and SC value. iQiyi had implemented encryption measures for its video content by setting a key (Key value), and the key (Key value) was not publicly disclosed.

On April 13, 2015, the plaintiff iQiyi, through notarization, used a decompilation tool and the "Wireshark" software to capture the access time (TimeID), video ID (VideoID), and client code (SRC value) when the "VST All-in-One" software played a video from the iQiyi website. After adding iQiyi's key (Key value), the SC value generated using the MD5 encryption algorithm in the order TimeID+Key+VideoID matched the SC value captured when the "VST All-in-One" software played the same video from the iQiyi website. Therefore, when playing videos sourced from the iQiyi website, the "VST All-in-One" software embedded iQiyi's key (Key value), thereby passing verification by iQiyi's server and being pushed the main content. The defendant Juwangshi argued that this key (Key value) was lawfully obtained from public channels.

The advertising placement fee calculation methods for the plaintiff iQiyi's website and clients include CPM billing and CPD billing. The former sells advertisements based on cost per thousand impressions, and the latter sells advertisements based on cost per day of publication. iQiyi's player includes an interface for counting the number of ad appearances, and advertisers settle accounts with iQiyi based on the statistical data.

The Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai held in the first instance:

Although the plaintiff iQiyi's business field is video provision, and the defendant Juwangshi's business scope is the development and sale of computer hardware and software, the "VST All-in-One" software developed and operated by Juwangshi is software that provides videos. Using the "VST All-in-One" software to watch video content sourced from iQiyi without watching pre-roll advertisements will lead iQiyi's users to choose to watch iQiyi's video content through the "VST All-in-One" software. This affects iQiyi's economic interests while bringing users to Juwangshi. Therefore, iQiyi and Juwangshi have a seesaw relationship in commercial interests, and the parties are in a competitive relationship.

The plaintiff iQiyi provides free videos to users in exchange for watching pre-roll advertisements, obtaining profit through advertisement play or by charging membership fees from members who are exempt from watching advertisements. iQiyi's aforementioned business model neither violates existing laws nor commercial ethics and should be protected by law. iQiyi has implemented encryption measures for its video content by setting a key (Key value), clearly indicating its refusal to allow others to share its video content arbitrarily. The defendant Juwangshi, by cracking iQiyi's verification algorithm, obtained the key (Key value), thereby circumventing iQiyi's pre-roll advertisements and directly accessing the main content for playback. Although it did not have a direct act of removing pre-roll advertisements, it objectively achieved the purpose of directly watching the main content without watching pre-roll advertisements. This can cause some network users who are unwilling to watch pre-roll advertisements and also unwilling to pay iQiyi's membership fee to switch to using the "VST All-in-One" software, thereby reducing iQiyi's user base and advertising revenue, harming iQiyi's legitimate rights and interests. Therefore, the act of circumventing iQiyi's advertisements and directly playing videos, achieved by the "VST All-in-One" software developed and operated by Juwangshi, violates the principle of good faith and generally accepted commercial ethics, harms iQiyi's legitimate interests, and constitutes unfair competition.

Accordingly, on October 14, 2015, the Yangpu District People's Court of Shanghai, in accordance with Articles 2(1), 2(2), and 20 of the Anti-Unfair Competition Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 15(1)(1), (6), (8), and 15(2) of the Tort Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment:

1. The defendant, Shenzhen Juwangshi Technology Co., Ltd., shall pay the plaintiff, Beijing iQiyi Technology Co., Ltd., compensation for economic losses of RMB 300,000 and reasonable expenses of RMB 60,000 within ten days from the date the judgment takes effect; 2. The defendant, Shenzhen Juwangshi Technology Co., Ltd., shall publish a statement on the top of the homepage of its official website (http://www.91vst.com/) for 72 consecutive hours to eliminate the impact of its unfair competition act.

After the first instance judgment was pronounced, Juwangshi refused to accept it and appealed to the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court.

The appellant Juwangshi appealed, arguing: The key (Key value) used by the "VST All-in-One" software originated from public information on the internet, and was not, as found by the first instance court, obtained by cracking the verification algorithm of the appellee iQiyi. The act of circumventing iQiyi's pre-roll advertisements and directly playing videos was caused by technical reasons; Juwangshi had no subjective intent. Accordingly, it requested the court to reverse the original judgment and render a new judgment dismissing all of iQiyi's original claims in the first instance.

The appellee iQiyi argued: iQiyi's key (Key value) has always been kept confidential and could not be obtained from public channels; the reason the appellant Juwangshi circumvented the pre-roll advertisements was that it actively pursued this result through technical means; the technology implemented by Juwangshi could arbitrarily obtain iQiyi's videos, causing harm and danger far greater than infringing the right of communication through information networks of a specific work. It requested the court to dismiss Juwangshi's appeal and uphold the original judgment.

The Shanghai Intellectual Property Court, upon second instance trial, confirmed the facts found in the first instance.

The Shanghai Intellectual Property Court held in the second instance:

The focus of the dispute in this case is: Whether the appellant Juwangshi, by cracking the verification algorithm of the appellee iQiyi, obtained the key (Key value) for the "VST All-in-One" software and implemented the act of circumventing the advertisements to directly play iQiyi's videos; and whether the act of circumventing the advertisements to directly play videos is legitimate.

The court held that: The appellant Juwangshi claimed that the key (Key value) used by the "VST All-in-One" software originated from public channels, and it needed to provide evidence to support this claim. However, Juwangshi failed to provide evidence to prove its assertion. On the contrary, the evidence provided by the appellee iQiyi can prove that iQiyi had implemented encryption measures for the videos it provided, and Juwangshi, by cracking iQiyi's verification algorithm, obtained the key (Key value) to generate the SC value for requesting video playback, achieving the purpose of directly obtaining video playback without watching pre-roll advertisements.

The business conduct of the appellee iQiyi, which relies on the "advertising + free video" model or the model of charging membership fees from users to seek commercial benefits through advertising fees and membership fees, should be protected by law. The act of circumventing the advertisements and directly playing iQiyi's videos was the result of the appellant Juwangshi adopting technical means. By virtue of this technology, Juwangshi enabled its users to watch iQiyi's videos without spending time or money costs. This will cause some of iQiyi's users to become Juwangshi's users and will lead to a decrease in iQiyi's advertising clicks and membership fee income. Juwangshi allowed its users to watch iQiyi's videos through its technology, but it did not pay operating costs such as copyright fees; those costs were still borne by iQiyi. Meanwhile, iQiyi, while paying the aforementioned costs, faces a loss of commercial benefits due to the decrease in user numbers and advertising clicks. Juwangshi, as the implementer of the technology, knew that the technology would result in its own gain at the expense of others, yet it still implemented the technology. This constitutes subjective intent, violates the principle of good faith and generally accepted commercial ethics, infringes upon iQiyi's legitimate business activities, and its act lacks legitimacy.

In summary, the first instance found the facts clearly and applied the law correctly, and should be affirmed. The appellant Juwangshi's appeal requests and the reasons thereof lack factual and legal basis and should be dismissed. Accordingly, on April 26, 2016, the Shanghai Intellectual Property Court, in accordance with Article 170(1)(1) and Article 175 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, rendered the following judgment:

Dismiss the appeal and affirm the original judgment.

This judgment is final.
